speaker: Doctor
text: I am Dr. Agent. I see you are presenting with dizziness, nausea, and imbalance. To understand the nature of your symptoms, have these episodes been sudden onset or gradual, and do they worsen when you change your head position?

speaker: Patient
text: 27-year-old male. The patient reports a sustained sensation of the room spinning since this morning, which is low grade and constant. He occasionally feels nauseous and has taken diphenhydramine to help him sleep, which also alleviates his symptoms slightly. He mentions recent increased intake of garlic due to trying to recover from a cold a few days ago. Past medical history is unremarkable.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) is less likely given the constant nature of the spinning; the clinical picture of constant vertigo, nausea, and slight relief with diphenhydramine strongly suggests Vestibular Neuritis or Labyrinthitis. Given the unilateral symptoms implied by the constant spinning, I am requesting a Vestibular Evoked Myogenic Potential (VEMP) test and a Hearing test to rule out inner ear involvement.
